\paragraph{Drafter's summary.} logit P(churn) = -1.15 + a sparse linear backbone over 33 inputs (day minutes +1.84 per SD, voicemail plan -0.87, international plan +0.76, international charge +0.69, voicemail messages +0.58, evening minutes +0.50, ...) + a service-call x low-day-usage gate + a 4+-calls hinge + exactly linear voicemail, state-offset and area-code units, all additive in the logit. The gate is a low-day-minutes hinge whose kink moves up with each customer-service call (median 147 day minutes at 0 calls, 215 at 4, 270 at 6), lowered by high evening charge and switched off in state:0, so with the direct day-minutes edge the logit is V-shaped in day minutes and frequent callers with low usage churn. Service calls act only through hinges. Train AUC 0.894, accuracy 0.896.

\paragraph{What resisted explanation.} Nothing structural: no hidden node needed splitting (13 input splits, 3 consolidations). Node 14653 (area code 408) is never active on train (dead); 252 (state:44 / very low international charge) is active on 100 rows with at most +0.03 logit. The gate under-predicts churn for frequent callers with low day usage (CSC$>$=4 and day minutes $<$160: 113 rows, model 0.52 vs empirical 0.88). The voicemail chain is exactly linear, and mean-ablating it raises train AUC (0.8944 -$>$ 0.8979): its extra voicemail-plan penalty slightly hurts ranking. closed\_\allowbreak{}form\_\allowbreak{}max\_\allowbreak{}abs\_\allowbreak{}err 0.043 (state\_\allowbreak{}offsets) is 3-significant-figure rounding on state one-hots (standardised values up to 8); the numeric function is exact (2.7e-15).

\subsection{Plain-language summary}\label{app:churn100-s2-c2:plain}
\noindent{\small\textit{AI-assisted draft for review (unverified). Each sentence cites the claims (C01, C02, \ldots) that back it; every cited claim was computed on the model and the training split and passed its automatic checks. Magnitudes are changes in predicted risk for a typical patient; confidence words follow the test-split check and n. The text describes what the model does, not the world.}}\par\smallskip
\paragraph{Summary (drafted).} For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 1\%; it adds up six parts: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, a voice-mail discount, state units, an area-code unit and a small Utah unit.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C051]}} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights, and daytime minutes count most: they raise a typical customer's chance of leaving steadily, from under 1\% at 112 to about 11\% at 249 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C053]}} An international plan takes the chance from about 1\% to about 14\%, a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1\%, and more voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1\% at 0 to about 4\% at 32 messages.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C052, C061, C056]}} A higher international charge, more evening minutes, a higher evening charge and more night-time minutes also raise it steadily, each by one to two points.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057, C059, C060, C065]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 5\% in Washington and in California, and to under 1\% in Hawaii (41 to 122 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C054, C055, C062]}} This part adds up two parts: customer-service calls combined with low daytime use, and a rise from 4 calls upwards.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103]}} Through it, daytime minutes lower the chance only while they stay below about 166 minutes (between 145 and 213 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 28\% at 91 minutes to about 1\% at 352 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C098]}} With an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, the chance is lowest at about 148 minutes of daytime use and higher either side: from about 1\% at 112 minutes to about 13\% at 249 minutes, against about 2\% to about 9\% at or below that charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C095]}} Customer-service calls add to it from 4 calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, from about 3\% at 0 calls to about 8\% at 4 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C099]}} This part reads the voice-mail plan and one state: through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to under 1\%, and customers in North Carolina get under 1\% instead of about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C119, C120]}} This part reads only the state: it raises a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to about 2\% in Washington and in Montana, and by less than a point in Kentucky and Ohio.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C125, C126, C127, C128]}} This part reads the area code and barely changes the predictions (by at most half a point).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C137]}} This small part reads the international charge and being in Utah, and barely changes the predictions (by at most 0.2 points).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C144]}}
\paragraph{The whole model.} The model adds up six parts into one score: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, a voice-mail discount, state units, an area-code unit and a small Utah unit.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C051]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made up of these six parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C051]}} Changing one input at a time across the whole model, an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1\% to about 14\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C001, C010]}} In Washington the chance is about 9\%, against about 1\% in West Virginia.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C003]}} More customer-service calls raise it slowly at first, then faster, from about 1\% at 0 calls to about 2\% at 3 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C011]}} The model ignores the daytime charge, evening calls, international minutes, night-time calls and the night-time charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C046, C047, C048, C049, C050]}}
\paragraph{Fixed-weight inputs.} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: daytime minutes, an international plan and voice-mail messages raise the chance of leaving, steadily for the minutes and messages, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C053, C052, C056, C061]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, daytime minutes take a typical customer steadily from under 1\% at 112 to about 11\% at 249 minutes, and an international plan from about 1\% to about 14\%; a voice-mail plan lowers the chance to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C053, C052, C061]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 5\% in Washington and in California, and to under 1\% in Hawaii (41 to 122 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C054, C055, C062]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C085]}}
\paragraph{Service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving with calls to customer service, from 4 calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster, and more so for customers with low daytime use, in an uneven way; it adds up two parts.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103, C099, C098]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made of two parts that are added: calls with low usage, and many service calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103]}} Through it, daytime minutes lower the chance only while they stay below about 166 minutes (between 145 and 213 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 28\% at 91 minutes to about 1\% at 352 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C098]}} Customer-service calls add to it from 4 calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, from about 3\% at 0 calls to about 8\% at 4 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C099]}} With an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, the chance is lowest at about 148 minutes of daytime use and higher either side: from about 1\% at 112 minutes to about 13\% at 249 minutes, against about 2\% to about 9\% at or below that charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C095]}}
\paragraph{Calls with low usage.} This part raises the chance of leaving for customers with low usage, more so when they call customer service: daytime minutes lower it only while they stay below about 166 minutes (between 145 and 213 minutes for different customers), and calls raise it, both in an uneven way.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C112, C106]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 3063 of 4000 training customers, 393 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, it changes the chance by less than a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C117]}} Through it, a typical customer's chance falls in an uneven way from about 28\% at 91 minutes of daytime use to about 1\% at 352 minutes, with no further fall past about 166 minutes (between 145 and 213 minutes for different customers).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C112]}} A higher international charge lowers it steadily up to about 2.95 US dollars (between 2.95 and 4.10 US dollars for different customers), then no further: for a typical such customer, from about 4\% to about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C115]}} Customer-service calls raise it in an uneven way, from about 1\% at 0 calls to about 2\% at 3 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C106]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C118]}}
\paragraph{Many service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving from 4 customer-service calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C122]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 318 of 4000 training customers, 159 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 7\% without it and about 12\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C123]}} Through it, the chance rises slowly at first, then faster: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical such customer's chance from about 1\% to about 2\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C122]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C124]}}
\paragraph{Voice-mail discount.} This part gives customers with a voice-mail plan a further discount on the chance of leaving.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C119]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to under 1\%, and customers in North Carolina get under 1\% instead of about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C119, C120]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C121]}}
\paragraph{State units.} This part reads only the state and raises the chance of leaving in a few states, most in Washington and Montana.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C125, C126]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a typical customer's chance goes from about 1\% to about 2\% in Washington and in Montana, and up by less than a point in Kentucky and Ohio.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C125, C126, C127, C128]}} In Arizona, Delaware, North Dakota and Nevada it lowers the chance by less than a tenth of a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C129, C130, C131, C132]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C133]}}
\paragraph{Area-code unit.} This part reads the area code and barely changes the predictions.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C137]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a typical customer's chance stays at about 1\% in area codes 408 and 510, as in area code 415.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C134, C135]}} Switching it off changes the predictions by at most half a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C137]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C138]}}
\paragraph{Small Utah unit.} This small part reads the international charge and being in Utah, and barely changes the predictions.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C144]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, the international charge barely changes the chance, which stays at about 1\% for the typical customer it acts on.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C139]}} Switching it off changes the predictions by at most 0.2 points.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C144]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C145]}}
\paragraph{Worth checking against what is known.} Worth checking: the state moves the chance by several points (for example Washington about 9\% and California about 5\%, Hawaii under 1\%), based on 41 to 122 training customers per state.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C003, C004, C012]}} Worth checking: the model treats a voice-mail plan as lowering the chance of leaving but more voice-mail messages as raising it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C010, C005]}} Worth checking: daytime minutes, the evening charge and the international charge raise the chance through the fixed-weight inputs but lower it through calls with low usage.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C053, C104, C060, C107, C057, C105]}}

\subsection{Coverage}\label{app:churn100-s2-c2:coverage}
Coverage is computed by the current code (the function behind the \texttt{get\_coverage} tool) under these conventions. \emph{Candidate nodes} are all nodes of the explained model state except the output nodes. A candidate node is \emph{covered} when some annotation of the hierarchy (a leaf, or a composition together with its descendants) contains it and all its enabled outgoing edges. \emph{Exact Null} parts, which have no effect on any output for any input, count as covered: nodes with no path to an output over enabled, non-zero-weight edges (disconnected inputs and dead ends), and edges that have zero weight or touch such a node. Compositional coverage is the fraction of required compositions present: every annotation except a single global root containing every output must have a parent; a parentless, childless annotation made only of Null nodes is exempt.
